about.label: About the canal
about.heading: Where old Chiang Mai meets the water
about.lead: Mae Kha Canal (คลองแม่ข่า) is one of Chiang Mai's historic waterways — once part of the Lanna kingdom's irrigation and transport network, now a living riverside neighbourhood.
about.paragraph1: For centuries the canal carried water from the western hills through the city, lining its banks with wooden houses, gardens, and small communities. As Chiang Mai grew, the waterway was neglected and polluted, and for a time it became little more than a forgotten ditch.
about.paragraph2: In recent decades local residents and the city have worked together to clean and revive Mae Kha. Today it is best known for its calm evening walking street, short boat rides, and a string of food stalls and cafés that turn the banks into an open-air kitchen after sunset.
about.quote: Walk slowly; the canal remembers more than the city does.

history.label: History
history.heading: From Lanna waterway to evening promenade
history.intro: The canal's story mirrors Chiang Mai's own — built for water, forgotten, then rediscovered.

blocks.title: Lanna origins
blocks.text: Mae Kha was dug as part of Chiang Mai's historic water system, carrying water from the western hills through the city for irrigation and daily life.

blocks.title: A working canal
blocks.text: For centuries it was a transport and washing route for riverside communities, with wooden houses and gardens along its banks.

blocks.title: Decline & revival
blocks.text: Urban growth and pollution choked the canal. In recent decades local residents and the city joined forces to clean it, planting banks and opening a riverside walking street.

legend.title: Why 'Mae Kha'?
legend.text: In northern Thai, 'Mae' means mother or river and 'Kha' names the stream — a reminder that the canal was long treated as a living relative of the city.

didYouKnow.title: Did you know?
didYouKnow.text: Chiang Mai's old city was laid out inside a square moat; Mae Kha was one of the outer canals that drained and fed the wider plain.

folklore.title: Water spirits
folklore.tale: Like many Thai waterways, locals once left small offerings to the river spirit (Phi Mae Nam) for safe passage and good fortune — a quiet tradition still remembered by older residents.
folklore.shrine: If you see a small spirit house or flower offering by the water, admire it from a distance and avoid disturbing it.

bestTime.title: Best time to visit
bestTime.intro: Chiang Mai has three distinct seasons that change the canal's mood.

seasons.name: Cool season
seasons.desc: Pleasant evenings and the clearest light — the most comfortable time to walk.

seasons.name: Hot season
seasons.desc: Warm nights; go early in the opening hours to avoid the heat.

seasons.name: Rainy season
seasons.desc: Lush banks and fewer crowds, but afternoon showers may pause boat rides.

items.title: Near water
items.desc: Keep children close to the edge; some banks are unrailed.

items.title: Boat rides
items.desc: Wear the life jacket provided and follow the operator's instructions.

items.title: Personal belongings
items.desc: Keep bags zipped in busy market areas.

hazeSeason.text: From roughly February to April, northern Thailand can have haze. Sensitive travellers may prefer the cool, clear months of December–January.

accessibility.title: Accessible for everyone

items.title: Wheelchair & stroller

items.title: Rest areas
items.desc: Shaded benches and cafés with seating.

items.title: Toilets

faqs.q: When is Mae Kha Canal open?
faqs.a: The canal and evening walking street are busiest from around 16:00 to 22:00. Daytime is quiet — most food stalls open in the late afternoon.
Walking the canal and browsing the market is free. Boat rides and food are paid separately.

faqs.q: How do I get there from the old city?
faqs.a: It is a short taxi, red songthaew, or bicycle ride to Haiya. Use a map app and set 'Mae Kha Canal'.
Yes for a first visit — a short ride offers a calm view of teak houses and lit bridges you cannot see from the path.
Very — flat paths, food for all ages, and boat rides, though supervise children near unrailed banks.
